skills.name: European powers on the Cameroon coast before annexation

note.text: Overseas contact developed before formal colonial rule. Portuguese arrivals were recorded on the coast in the fifteenth century; later British, German and other trading connections grew. Merchants sought products and access, while missions pursued religious and educational activities. African traders and rulers negotiated these relationships and protected their own interests. Coastal commerce was not the same thing as possession of the whole interior. The existence of a European ship or mission station does not establish that all local communities had surrendered sovereignty.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Duala traders acted between inland producers and overseas firms. British commercial and missionary ties were established before the German claim in {1884}. German firms also built interests on the coast. Comparing their roles helps explain later rivalry, but European records must be read alongside evidence of African choices and authority.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Distinguish contact, trade, mission work and formal political control. Ask what area a source actually describes. Do not use the colonial language of discovery to imply that land was unknown to its inhabitants. Identify the interests and standpoint of the person writing the record.
